transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Ellen Gomez (Redwood CSM) — Amir Kahn (Zephyrus Head of MLOps), Sofia Ruiz (Zephyrus CTO), Liam O'Connor (Platform Eng), Priya Verma (SRE)

Optional auto sections (generated by call):
Summary: Scoping POC for capacity sizing and autoscaling. Focus areas: reserved GPUs for baseline throughput, burst strategy for peak events, fallback policies to hosted model variants, success criteria (latency & availability), benchmarks and timeline (2 week POC with benchmark run).
Topics: capacity sizing, burst capacity, reserved vs hosted, fallback to smaller model or hosted API, KV cache warmup, quantization profile, security and network constraints, timeline
Action items: see metadata action_items above

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, quick intro from our side — I'm Maya, AE on the account, Ravi is our SE and Ellen's on CSM.
[00:10] Amir Kahn: Hi — Amir here. Thanks. We want to focus on POC for capacity and autoscale so we can validate latency and cost tradeoffs.
[00:18] Ravi Patel: Great. High level — we usually run a 2-week POC for capacity and autoscale where we provision reserved GPUs for baseline, enable burst capacity for spikes, and validate fallback routing to lighter model variants or Redwood's hosted endpoints if needed.
[00:32] Sofia Ruiz: Two weeks sounds fine. Our initial targets: p95 latency under 800 ms for typical prompts and 99% availability during business hours. We also want to keep unit cost below X (she mumbles, unclear), so cost/latency tradeoff matters.
[00:50] Maya Chen: Yep, totally. Can you share current traffic profile? QPS distribution, percentiles, and typical prompt length?
[00:58] Amir Kahn: We have a 24 hour trace — average 12 QPS, 95th peeks to 95 QPS, and a couple of 10-minute spikes hitting ~220 QPS during nightly batch jobs. Prompt lengths are mixed: median 120 tokens, 95th around 700 tokens.
[01:18] Ravi Patel: Ok that's helpful. For that profile we typically recommend reserving a baseline pool sized for your 95 QPS steady peaks — that way you get predictable latency. For the longer sequences we'll lean on batching and KV cache to save tokens and latency.
[01:34] Liam O'Connor: Are you saying reserved GPUs for the 95 QPS, and then burst to additional GPUs for the 220 QPS spikes? How fast is the burst spin-up?
[01:42] Ravi Patel: Good question. For Dedicated we have warm pools and cold pools. Warm pool spin-up is on the order of ~90 seconds to a couple minutes depending on model and init. For ultra-fast bursts we recommend a hybrid: keep a small hot pool of cheaper GPUs or small-model replicas and then spin additional full GPUs; plus a fallback policy to route non-critical traffic to the hosted Redwood API (or to a distilled quantized variant) to avoid cold-start latency.
[02:06] Priya Verma: Our constraints: all outbound must go through corporate proxies, and any burst VMs must be approved by network. Also we need to ensure keys never leave our KMS — is that supported?
[02:16] Maya Chen: Yes, for Private we can integrate with your KMS/HSM. For Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS in the VPC offering; we can sign an addendum for key controls.
[02:25] Sofia Ruiz: For the POC are you proposing Redwood Private or Dedicated? We're evaluating both but prefer to start on Dedicated if it reduces time to test.
[02:33] Ravi Patel: Dedicated is usually faster for a POC because we can spin up reserved capacity in the region and you get the same runtime and tooling. Private adds network setup that can add a few days. For the burst strategy we can configure a reserved baseline (eg 4 A100s) and a burst pool that can go to 8 or 12 using spot/burst capacity depending on commit.
[02:50] Amir Kahn: Can you give a concrete sizing recommendation for our numbers? 12 avg, 95 steady, 220 spike, prompt lengths median 120 / 95th 700.
[02:58] Ravi Patel: Based on our bench rules of thumb: a single A100 (40GB) serving 8–12 concurrent requests for medium prompts with optimized kernels. For your 95 QPS at p95 < 800 ms, I'd recommend reserving 4 x A100s as baseline (gives headroom with batching), with a hot small-model fleet of 2 x T4-like instances or 2 q4_0 quantized replicas for ultra-low-latency small requests. Then burst to an additional 4 GPUs (so total 8) during peaks. If you need headroom up to 220 QPS we can have burst autoscale to 12 GPUs but cost increases.
[03:32] Sofia Ruiz: That baseline seems pricey. How do we test cheaper quantized profiles?
[03:36] Ravi Patel: We'll run benchmark sweeps: full FP16, int8 quantized, and q4_0 style lower-precision variants. Our Redwood Optimize suggestions will show cost/latency tradeoffs. In the POC we'll run side-by-side benchmarks to measure tokens/sec, latency p50/p95/p99, and cost per 1k tokens.
[03:54] Amir Kahn: On fallback policies: we want user-facing critical paths never to degrade below p95 1s. Non-critical tasks (background summarization) can be downgraded. How would you configure that?
[04:06] Ravi Patel: You define route policies in the control plane: critical route -> baseline model pinned to reserved pool; background route -> can be routed to quantized variant or hosted API. We can also set automatic fallback: if reserved pool latency exceeds threshold or errors spike, automatically route to hosted endpoint with higher cost but guaranteed availability. We'll test failover during the POC by simulating GPU drains.
[04:26] Maya Chen: I'll note that for the POC success criteria we should record exact metrics: p95 latency < 800ms for critical route, 99% availability business hours, and cost per 1k tokens under your target (customer to confirm X). Also we want warmed KV cache hit rate above 60% for conversational flows.
[04:44] Priya Verma: Do you support prefix caching across pods? We need consistent cache warming across autoscaled instances so first requests don't blow latency.
[04:52] Ravi Patel: We do prefix/KV cache and we can pre-warm caches during benchmark runs. For autoscale events we recommend slow ramp-up or sticky sessions so that hot caches follow sticky users; otherwise you see temporary p99 spikes.
[05:06] Liam O'Connor: For the benchmark harness — what do you need from us?
[05:10] Ravi Patel: Two things: 1) sample traffic trace (we asked for 24h), 2) the top 50 prompts and their expected sequence lengths. We'll create a synthetic load generator that replays the trace with realistic think times and token lengths. We'll run against baseline models and quantized variants. We'll also simulate network constraints you mentioned.
[05:30] Sofia Ruiz: Timeline? When can we run the POC?
[05:33] Maya Chen: If we get the sample trace and sign the POC SoW this week, we can provision Dedicated baseline capacity and run the first bench in ~3 business days — so kickoff benchmark run week of 2026-08-17. Full 2-week POC wraps by end of month.
[05:46] Amir Kahn: Ok that fits. Are there typical failure modes we should be aware of during burst?
[05:51] Ravi Patel: Yes: cold start latency on new GPUs, cache miss storms, and queuing that increases p99. Our mitigations: warm pools, sticky sessions, backpressure at the router with graceful retries, and rate-limited fallback to hosted endpoints. Also kernel selection: if you have long sequences, choose kernels tuned for kv cache and attention recompute — our runtime picks those automatically but some model shims are better with specific compile flags.
[06:18] Maya Chen: We should also cover security checklist — SOC2, encryption at rest and transit, SSO/SAML, RBAC. Priya — are there any must-haves for Zephyrus?
[06:27] Priya Verma: SOC2 report required, SAML SSO, and KMS integration — cannot export plaintext keys. Also audit logs retained 1 year.
[06:33] Ellen Gomez: We have a security pack and SOC2 summary we can share. For KMS we can do customer-managed keys in Private and Dedicated in VPC. I'll attach the guide.
[06:41] Amir Kahn: Great. On cost, can you show an example cost table for the baseline 4 A100 + bursts?
[06:47] Maya Chen: We'll include a pricing example in the SoW. Rough example in chat: baseline 4 x A100 reserved = monthly commit X, burst per-hour = Y, and hosted fallbacks billed per-token. We'll put exact numbers in the doc.
[06:58] Sofia Ruiz: What about metrics and observability during the POC? We need token-level cost, per-route latency breakdown, and traces.
[07:06] Ravi Patel: Console exposes token-level cost, per-route dashboards, per-model latency distributions, and tracing hooks you can instrument. For the POC we'll grant you full access to the console and create a dedicated dashboard for the benchmarks.
[07:16] Amir Kahn: Are there any constraints on the quantized models — like quality regressions? We need to evaluate output quality as well as latency/cost.
[07:24] Ravi Patel: Correct — we'll run side-by-side evaluated prompts and measure quality regressions using your test set and our eval harness (ROUGE/BLEU and human spot checks). We'll include quality thresholds in the success criteria.
[07:36] Maya Chen: To recap: success criteria: p95 < 800ms for critical route, 99% availability BH, quality regression < 5% on eval set, and cost per 1k tokens under customer's target. Baseline sizing: 4 x A100 reserved, hot pool of 2 small-model replicas, burst up to 8-12 GPUs depending on tolerance. Benchmarks: FP16, int8/q4 variants, KV cache warmup tests, simulated GPU drains for failover. Timeline: samples + SoW this week, kickoff bench 2026-08-17, POC duration 2 weeks.
[08:04] Sofia Ruiz: Sounds good. One more question re: autoscaling policy — what metrics drive scaling? Latency SLO breaches or queue depth?
[08:13] Ravi Patel: We support policy-based scaling: CPU/GPU utilization, request queue depth, or observed latency threshold. For your use-case I'd recommend queue-depth + p95 latency as triggers so we don't oscillate on short blips. We'll tune cooldown windows in the POC.
[08:29] Priya Verma: For network approvals — we'll need a list of outbound IPs and ports. Can you provide that?
[08:35] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll attach the network allowlist and cloud region info with the SoW.
[08:40] Liam O'Connor: If we simulate a GPU drain, you mentioned fallback to hosted — won't that leak PII? We need to ensure data residency.
[08:48] Ravi Patel: Good catch. Fallback to hosted should be restricted to anonymized or non-PII paths. For sensitive payloads we can configure the route to fail closed (reject) or fall back to a private smaller model running in your VPC. We'll document options and default to fail-closed unless you allow hosted fallback.
[09:05] Amir Kahn: Ok let's do fail-closed for critical user paths and hosted fallback allowed for background tasks.
[09:11] Maya Chen: Noted. Any other blockers?
[09:14] Sofia Ruiz: Just pricing details and SoW.
[09:17] Maya Chen: We'll send those.
[09:19] [crosstalk — brief confirmations]
[09:22] Sofia Ruiz: Quick note — can you include an example runbook for when the autoscaler misbehaves? We want an on-call playbook.
[09:29] Ravi Patel: Sure — we'll include an incident playbook: detect, failover, rollback, and how to force-route. We'll also hand-run a simulated incident during the POC.
[09:38] Amir Kahn: Great.
[09:40] Maya Chen: Ok I'll summarize next steps in email. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
